title: PaymentCredential
description:
What a Credential Provider returns in place of an instrument: something spendable for one checkout and useless for any other. The agent never sees a PAN, and nothing here is one — this project enrols no real card and the Credential Provider is mocked, which is a hard constraint of the ecosystem rather than a shortcut, since no public sandbox lets a non-PSP enrol a card into an AP2 flow.

The scoping is the whole point. A credential that could pay for any checkout would move the trust boundary back to wherever it is stored; one bound to a single checkout is worth no more to a thief than the purchase the user already approved.

token.description: The spendable value, opaque to everyone but the Credential Provider that minted it and the Merchant Payment Processor that redeems it. Never a PAN, never derived from one.

checkout_hash.description: base64url digest of the checkout this credential may pay for — the same value the Checkout Mandate and the Payment Mandate carry. A Merchant Payment Processor presented with a credential whose scope does not match the checkout being paid for must reject it as credential_scope_mismatch.
checkout_hash.$comment: One digest, now in three places: the Checkout Mandate says the user authorised this purchase, the Payment Mandate says the agent may pay for it, and this says the money is only good for it. Each is a separate signature by a separate party, and the shared value is what makes them one transaction rather than three assertions.

expires_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp after which this credential must not be redeemed. A scoped credential that never expires is a scoped credential somebody can sit on.
